comics.title: Vintage
comics.alt: A restaurant cartoon. A sommelier with a napkin on his arm presents a dusty, cobwebbed Nvidia H100 chip on a cradle to a seated diner with a candle and a wine glass. A chalkboard lists 'H100, vintage 2022, $3.11/hr, up' and 'NVDA, vintage Oct., minus 50%, down'.
comics.caption: "The 2022 is up nearly sixty percent this year, sir. The one from October, I'm afraid, has turned."

story.title: GPU prices are rising for Nvidia's older chips even as the stock keeps going down: Chart of the Day

rationale.why_this_story: The week had heavier news (elections, Hormuz, COP31), but much of it is hard to joke about without punching down or flattening real suffering. This story has a built-in joke: Yahoo Finance itself compares H100 rental prices to fine wine, and the target is the AI-hardware hype machine.
rationale.how_the_joke_works: A New Yorker-style single panel. The wine-service ritual is applied to a GPU, and the caption does the vintage-versus-spoiled turn on 'the one from October', a stock down nearly half. Facts (about 60% rental rise, stock roughly halved since October) come from the article.
rationale.intended_landing: A small, dry laugh of recognition that the AI trade has become a collectible: the old hardware appreciates like claret while the company's stock goes off like milk. Rejected: a Delta outage gag and Iowa's explosives story, both funny but less surprising.

comics.title: Resignation Pending Review
comics.alt: A boardroom with two board members at a long table beside an empty red leather chair with a yellow sticky note reading RESIGNED stuck on its back. Through the window, a small crowd holds signs reading BRING JENSEN BACK, backed by Elon.
comics.caption: "Technically he resigned, but I'm told that's 'under review by his friends.'"

story.title: Jensen Huang weighs comeback as Nvidia CEO as allies lobby board, FT reports; Bessent calls for 'dramatic shakeup'

rationale.why_this_story: Other candidates were the FAA funding fight (Duffy asks for money Democrats say is already there) and Russian diesel under the Trump deal. I chose this because the powerful are the whole cast: billionaires and shareholders lobbying a board to undo a resignation. I stayed on that and left the scandal's personal details out.
rationale.how_the_joke_works: Single-panel, New Yorker style, because the joke is a contrast: a sticky note saying RESIGNED on an empty chair, and a crowd outside treating it as a draft state. The caption is a board member dryly reporting that a resignation is now subject to appeal by the executive's wealthy friends. Flat colours keep it legible on a phone.
rationale.intended_landing: A rueful nod: at the top of the economy, consequences look like a status you can lobby to change. The sticky note is the gag, since it is the flimsiest possible way to mark the end of a career, and the crowd outside is already peeling it off.

comics.title: Bigger and Stronger
comics.alt: A single-panel cartoon. A ship tilts, half sunk, beside a large iceberg with a gash in its hull. On deck a smiling captain shouts through a megaphone: 'We will be back, bigger and stronger than ever!' Beside him, a grim man wearing a Chief of Staff badge holds up a chart reading 'New course: same iceberg, faster'. Passengers wave from the water, near a floating sign: 'The voters just didn't get it'.
comics.caption: “The iceberg was a big factor, so I’ve put its biggest fan in charge of steering.”

story.title: Trump vows comeback as bitter showdown with Congress looms

rationale.why_this_story: The week was crowded: Iran strike talk, a Georgia vote-count error, Jensen Huang's affair admission, a podcast losing sponsors. This one had a clean contradiction in one article: Trump vows to come back 'BIGGER AND STRONGER' after the midterm loss, while appointing Stephen Miller chief of staff, though analysts link his immigration policy to the defeat. The Georgia story was a closer call but turns on a technical error, which is hard to draw.
rationale.how_the_joke_works: The idea is a disaster metaphor taken literally. The loss is the iceberg, the ship is the party, and a triumphant captain is promoting the navigator who chose the route. 'Same iceberg, faster' states the real strategy, doubling down, as a ship's chart. The sign blaming the voters nods to Trump's remark that his supporters likely didn't vote. I chose one panel because the joke is a single contrast: the words say comeback, the picture says sinking. The style is simple flat cartoon figures.
rationale.intended_landing: The recognition that after a defeat the loudest promise is a bigger version of what just failed, and that the consequences land on the passengers in the water rather than the captain. The target is a powerful leader and his team's strategy, not voters of either party. The figures are generic, with the Chief of Staff badge the only specific nod. I'd like readers across the spectrum to see the pattern, which any losing side can fall into.

comics.title: Frozen Assets
comics.alt: A single-panel cartoon on a harbour quay. Behind, a vast grey superyacht with three towering masts is moored; air-conditioning units on its deck blast cold air, icicles hang from the rail, and two tiny workers on ropes scrub the hull. In front, a beaming official in a tricolour sash gestures up at it for a sceptical reporter taking notes. A sign reads: SEQUESTERED. Upkeep: $30,000 a day. Paid by: taxpayers.
comics.caption: “Make no mistake: his assets are frozen. We run the air-conditioning around the clock.”

story.title: Italian taxpayers are paying millions to keep Russian yachts afloat

rationale.why_this_story: The week's Yahoo News front page was wall-to-wall midterms and Iran strikes, which are important but hard to say anything new about in one panel the day before the vote. This CNN piece had a self-contained absurdity: Italian law says a seized ship can't be left to rot, so since 2022 Italian taxpayers have paid about $30,000 a day for crew, fuel, cleaning and security on one sanctioned oligarch's $600 million yacht in Trieste, plus air-conditioning on the seized yachts to stop mould. I also weighed Grok's usage limits (on Yahoo Finance, so out of bounds) and the Trump arch ruling.
rationale.how_the_joke_works: It hangs on one pun that turns out to be literally true. 'Frozen assets' is the official language of sanctions, and the article says the yachts' air-conditioning runs to stop mould. So a proud official boasting about how tough the punishment is ends up describing a valet service. The drawing makes the pun physical (icicles, cold air) and the sign states the real bill. A New Yorker-style single panel fits because the whole joke is one line said with a straight face. The style is flat, clean line work with muted harbour colours.
rationale.intended_landing: The recognition that a punishment can quietly turn into a service for the person being punished, with the bill landing on everyone else. The mayor himself said it may end up cheaper for the oligarch to buy a new yacht than to repay Italy's costs. The target is the sanctions machinery and the oligarchs it was meant to hurt, not the Italians stuck paying for it, which is why the reporter looks unconvinced and the sign names who pays.
